chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah from Mu'awiya from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
He said: 'The Muhrim (person in Hajj/Umrah state of consecration) does not take from the hair of the Hallal (non-Muhrim).'
The Sheikh (peace be upon him) said: 'If the Muhrim hunts an ostrich and kills it, then upon him is a Bathanah (a specific sacrificial animal, typically a camel or cow).

key_terms.اَلْحَلاَلُ: A person not in the state of consecration
key_terms.اَلْمُحْرِمُ: The pilgrim in a state of consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.بَدَنَةٌ: A specific type of sacrificial animal, usually a camel or cow, used as expiation

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for a pilgrim who kills an ostrich during Hajj?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the specific legal consequences for a pilgrim (*Muhrim*) who violates the sanctity of the sacred state, citing the chain of transmission through Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id. It establishes that while taking hair from a non-consecrated person is prohibited, hunting and killing an ostrich incurs a specific expiation (*Badanah*), illustrating the detailed jurisprudential distinctions in Shia fiqh regarding accidental versus intentional violations of Hajj restrictions. The mention of Shaykh al-Tusi highlights the classical authority of this ruling within the Twelver scholarly tradition.
